sk-64db8f92.stem: Which notch at the distal end of the radius articulates with the head of the ulna?
sk-64db8f92.explanation: At the distal radio-ulnar joint the ulnar head sits in the ulnar notch of the radius; in pronation and supination the radius rotates around this fixed ulnar head. The joint is supported by the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).

sk-814e4ce2.stem: What is the order of the distal row of carpal bones from radial to ulnar?
sk-814e4ce2.explanation: From lateral to medial the distal row is the trapezium (thumb side), trapezoid, capitate (the largest) and hamate. The proximal row is the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform.

sk-592c5eaa.stem: Kienböck's disease is avascular necrosis of which bone?
sk-592c5eaa.explanation: Kienböck's disease is avascular necrosis of the lunate; negative ulnar variance (a short ulna) is a risk factor. Idiopathic necrosis of the scaphoid is Preiser's disease, of the femoral head Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, and of the navicular of the foot Köhler's disease.
notes: It has no eponymous necrosis of its own.
It is the site of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease.
It is the site of Preiser's disease.
It is the site of Köhler's disease.

sk-dbb3bf24.stem: Which structures attach to the hook of the hamate?
options: Abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis
The flexor retinaculum and the hypothenar flexor and opponens digiti minimi
Extensor retinaculum and extensor carpi ulnaris
sk-dbb3bf24.explanation: The hook of the hamate is the inferomedial attachment of the flexor retinaculum; flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi also arise from it. The hook is the lateral boundary of Guyon's canal; it can break in golf and baseball and affect the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

sk-d7b7ddde.stem: Which is the shortest and most mobile metacarpal?
sk-d7b7ddde.explanation: The thumb metacarpal forms a saddle joint with the trapezium, allowing opposition. The 2nd and 3rd metacarpals are the most fixed (the 'fixed unit' of the hand); the base of the 3rd metacarpal carries a styloid process.

sk-a9ffa742.stem: Which structures attach to the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)?
options: Sartorius, tensor fasciae latae and the inguinal ligament
Straight head of rectus femoris and the iliofemoral ligament
Internal oblique and the lacunar ligament
sk-a9ffa742.explanation: Sartorius and TFL arise from the ASIS, and the inguinal ligament runs from it to the pubic tubercle. The straight head of rectus femoris and the iliofemoral ligament attach to the AIIS. In adolescent athletes sartorius can avulse the ASIS and rectus femoris the AIIS.
notes: The lacunar ligament extends to the pubis.
These belong to the iliac fossa and psoas.

sk-c9a721e5.stem: Which of the following does NOT arise from the ischial tuberosity?
sk-c9a721e5.explanation: The short head arises from the lateral lip of the linea aspera and crosses only the knee. The ischial tuberosity is the 'sitting bone'; the hamstrings and the vertical fibres of adductor magnus arise from it, and the sacrotuberous ligament attaches to it.

sk-5fd892d5.stem: Which artery provides the main blood supply to the femoral head in adults?
options: The artery in the ligament of the head of the femur
Perforating branches of the profunda femoris
sk-5fd892d5.explanation: In adults the femoral head is supplied mainly by the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery ascending along the neck. In intracapsular (subcapital) fractures these branches are torn and avascular necrosis can develop; the artery of the ligament of the head contributes little in adults.

sk-3ce542da.stem: What is the approximate neck–shaft angle of the femur in adults?
sk-3ce542da.explanation: The neck–shaft angle is about 150° at birth and falls to around 125° in adults. A marked increase is called coxa valga and a decrease coxa vara; it is slightly smaller in women because of the wider pelvis.

sk-2bd1341c.stem: Which of the following muscles does NOT arise from the linea aspera?
sk-2bd1341c.explanation: Vastus intermedius arises from the anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft. Vastus lateralis and the short head of biceps femoris arise from the lateral lip of the linea aspera and vastus medialis from the medial lip; the adductors insert into the linea aspera.

sk-438ad979.stem: Which structure attaches to Gerdy's tubercle?
sk-438ad979.explanation: Gerdy's tubercle is on the anterolateral surface of the lateral condyle of the tibia; the iliotibial band attaches to it. The patellar ligament attaches to the tibial tuberosity, the pes anserinus to the upper medial tibia and the lateral collateral ligament to the fibular head.

sk-eede538b.stem: Which structures attach to the head of the fibula?
options: Pes anserinus and the tibial collateral ligament
Iliotibial tract and tensor fasciae latae
The biceps femoris tendon and the fibular collateral ligament
sk-eede538b.explanation: The biceps femoris tendon and the lateral collateral ligament attach to the fibular head; the common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck just below and passes forwards. This is why foot drop can develop in fibular neck fractures.

sk-7f55ff47.stem: Which statement about the patella is true?
options: It is fully ossified at birth
It lies outside the knee joint cavity
It is the largest sesamoid bone in the body and develops within the quadriceps tendon
On its posterior surface the medial facet is larger than the lateral
It attaches to the medial condyle of the tibia through the patellar ligament
sk-7f55ff47.explanation: The patella lengthens the lever arm of quadriceps and increases the power of extension. On its posterior surface the lateral facet is wider; it is connected to the tibial tuberosity by the patellar ligament and its posterior surface faces the joint cavity. It begins to ossify between 3 and 6 years of age.

sk-048b1450.stem: What does a Segond fracture indicate?
options: Avulsion at the edge of the lateral tibial plateau; it accompanies an anterior cruciate ligament tear
Calcification at the femoral attachment of the medial collateral ligament
A fibular head fracture accompanying a posterior cruciate ligament tear
An osteochondral fracture in lateral dislocation of the patella
Separation of the tibial tuberosity due to apophysitis
sk-048b1450.explanation: A Segond fracture is a small bone fragment pulled off the lateral tibial plateau by the anterolateral capsule/ligament in internal rotation and varus stress of the knee; although small on X-ray, it strongly suggests an anterior cruciate ligament tear. Calcification of the medial collateral ligament is Pellegrini–Stieda; apophysitis of the tuberosity is Osgood–Schlatter.

sk-ff3caabb.stem: Which part of the talus takes part in the ankle (talocrural) joint?
sk-ff3caabb.explanation: The trochlea of the talus sits in the mortise formed by the lower surface of the tibia and the two malleoli. Because the trochlea is wider in front, the joint is most stable in dorsiflexion. The head of the talus articulates with the navicular.

sk-e6838352.stem: Which accessory bone results from the lateral tubercle of the posterior process of the talus remaining separate?
sk-e6838352.explanation: The os trigonum results from non-fusion of the lateral tubercle of the posterior process of the talus; in ballet dancers and footballers it can cause posterior ankle impingement in forced plantarflexion.

sk-fad5735d.stem: The sinus tarsi is the space between which two bones?
sk-fad5735d.explanation: The sinus tarsi is a laterally opening canal formed by the sulcus tali under the neck of the talus and the sulcus calcanei on top of the calcaneus; it contains the strong interosseous talocalcaneal ligament, and extensor digitorum brevis arises in front of it.

sk-216c2bbd.stem: Which bones form the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot?
options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms and metatarsals 1–3
The cuneiforms and the metatarsal bases
sk-216c2bbd.explanation: The lateral arch is low and close to the ground; it matters for weight bearing, and its keystone is the cuboid. The medial arch is higher and formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms and metatarsals 1–3.
notes: This describes the medial longitudinal arch.
The talus does not take part in the lateral arch.

sk-d2649154.stem: In the first weeks of military training, a young recruit develops forefoot pain after long marches; X-ray shows a stress fracture of the shaft of the 2nd metatarsal. What is this fracture commonly called?
sk-d2649154.explanation: Repeated loading causes a stress fracture of the 2nd metatarsal, the thinnest and longest metatarsal; the first X-rays may be normal and callus appears after a few weeks. A Jones fracture is at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction of the 5th metatarsal.

sk-1c850577.stem: Which statement about the Jones fracture is true?
options: It is a fracture of the neck of the talus
It occurs at the head of the 1st metatarsal
It is an avulsion of the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal by fibularis brevis
It occurs at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction of the 5th metatarsal and has a high risk of non-union
It is a stress fracture of the calcaneus
sk-1c850577.explanation: The Jones fracture lies 1.5–3 cm distal to the tuberosity in a poorly vascularised 'watershed' zone; non-union is common and surgery may be needed. A tuberosity avulsion (pseudo-Jones) results from the pull of fibularis brevis in inversion and usually heals well.

sk-251ed70f.stem: Which tendon attaches to the calcaneal tuberosity?
sk-251ed70f.explanation: The Achilles tendon, the common tendon of gastrocnemius and soleus, attaches to the middle of the posterior surface of the heel; it is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. The zone 2–6 cm above its insertion has the poorest blood supply and is where rupture is most common.
